catalog_quote: 1.1. PHONEMIC INVENTORY Konyak has two types of phonemes. i. Tones (Suprasegmental phonemes), and ii. Vowels and Consonants (Segmental Phonemes). I. Tones: Konyak has three tones. They are: i. Rising tone which is represented with [ ʹ ] on the vowel; ii. Falling tone which is represented with [ ` ] on the vowel; and iii. Level tone which is left unmarked. ... [p. 6] Altogether there are 27 phonemes (three suprasegmentals plus 24 segmentals). ... 1. Tones: Rising é `dry up' (as water) šám `slow' (very) ká `kick' / Falling è `say' šàm `gong' (Konyak) kà `split' / Level e `he' šam `mud' ka `open' (mouth) ... [Introduction] Scope of the present work: This work attempts to provide a comprehensive analysis of the language basically through structural model. However, in this study discussion of supra-segmental features except for Tones is not undertaken.

new_statements.quote: p. 132: "Tobu syllable requires two elements: an obligatory vowel, a tone and one or two optional elements. Both onset and coda are not obligatory. All vowels constitute the nucleus of a syllable, and they are obligatory and act as the tone-bearing unit. [...] Three tones are detected in Tobu. It represents the initial analysis of tone in Tobu, which has been found to exhibit one contour tone-a high falling tone-and two register tones-a mid-tone and a low tone." p. 117: "Walling and Besa (2024) have identified three register tones in Standard Konyak: high, low, and mid. In contrast, this research has found that Tobu features one contour tone and two register tones: high-falling, mid, and low." pp. 58-59: "Tobu features sesquisyllables where the first syllable is short followed by a long syllable in a word. The first short syllable lacks coda and immediately followed by a more prominent syllable"

Adds: three register tones for Standard Konyak per the Walling & Besa grammar, a different (contour + register) system for Tobu, the vowel nucleus as tone-bearing unit, and sesquisyllables with a 'more prominent' major syllable in Tobu only. No stress placement is given, so it neither contradicts nor supplies a stress rule. new_statements.rule_in_words: Konyak (both the Tobu variety and Standard/Wakching Konyak) is described as a tone language: every syllable nucleus carries a lexically and grammatically contrastive tone (Tobu: high-falling, mid, low; Standard Konyak per Walling & Besa: high, mid, low register tones). The thesis contains no statement on word stress or accent for Konyak; the word 'stress' occurs only in the ch. 2 review of general phonology textbooks (pp. 21-28). The only prominence remark is that in Tobu sesquisyllables the short codaless first syllable is followed by 'a more prominent syllable' (the full, tone-bearing major syllable); Standard Konyak is said to lack sesquisyllables (p. 136).
new_statements.exceptions: Tobu high (level) tone is heard in a few items but is inconsistent across speakers, so its phonemic status is left open (p. 132); Tobu and Standard Konyak are stated to be mutually unintelligible and to differ in tone inventory (p. 118).
new_statements.identity_note: Besa 2025 describes the Tobu area variety (Tobu circle, Mon district, Nagaland) and compares it with Standard Konyak = the Wakching variety adopted as the tribe's common language in 1951 (thesis ch. 1 pp. 8-9); the two are stated to be mutually unintelligible. The Walling & Besa 2025 grammar (index 0) describes Standard (Wakching) Konyak according to the thesis. French 1983 (index 1) uses Wakching Konyak as one of seven Northern Naga dialects in a comparative reconstruction. Nagaraja 2010 (already held by the project) is a grammar of Konyak proper.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held scans ( p. 5, p. 6) and the scope sentence is verbatim in the seller-page text we hold; all three are now also confirmed in the complete book. (2) Deciding source is the standard reference grammar (Nagaraja 2010, CIIL, x+182 pp., Glottolog 'grammar'), not a secondary summary; the full text, downloaded now from the Internet Archive (open, CC BY-NC), contains no word-stress rule anywhere and adds that every syllable bears exactly one of the three tones, which supports the tonal / domain not stated by the source coding. (3) Nothing found contradicts the classification; the only plausibly better source is the print-only Walling & Besa 2025 grammar, whose prosody content is unknown
